title: broadcast man-memory n=16: S out, one-hot decode, R back

regions.name: input
regions.note: the problem's own stream: `0 addr` (READ) / `1 addr value` (WRITE)

regions.name: router / broadcaster
regions.note: `r` the op and branch on it. Each lane then reads the address and builds `1 << addr` with `M 1 {`, and `S` writes that into EVERY outgoing pipe at once. A READ then broadcasts 0; a WRITE broadcasts 1 and the value. This room owns no other outgoing pipe on purpose — `S` would broadcast into it too, which is why answers go through the collector instead.

regions.name: router spans the field
regions.note: empty, and load-bearing: a pipe's first cell must sit against its source room's wall. With a four-row router the lower bands' pipes parsed with no source at all and those cells bound a neighbour's pipe instead.

regions.name: cell field (ONE room)
regions.note: all 16 cells share this room. Five rows each: return corridor, main line, READ tail, WRITE lane, WRITE store. Columns 0-1 are the spawner's.

regions.name: cell addr 0
regions.note: holds address 0 in its man's B. `b` moves the broadcast word to BP, then 0 x `]` shifts bit 0 down to bit 0 and `x` turns on it — all BP-only, so B is never touched. READ: `W M s`. WRITE: `r` then `M`.

regions.name: collector
regions.note: `R` reads from ANY incoming pipe, so the answer needs no addressing at all — the many-to-one teleport. Spanning the field's rows is what makes every answer pipe a two-cell stub instead of a fan-out corridor.

regions.name: output
regions.note: one word per READ

circles.name: one-hot in one glyph
circles.note: A=1, B=addr, so `{` (A << B) is the whole address decoder
